sections.title: Advanced Strategy for Level 3
sections.content: In Level 3, questions are not limited to simply forming a chain. It includes reverse checking, conditional symbol changes, missing statement insertion, and abstract logical structures. Solutions usually take 4–6 steps, and option elimination becomes very important.

sections.title: Reverse Inequalities Concept
sections.content: Question: In which expression will 'H > J' be definitely true and 'K ≤ G' be definitely false? Solution: First build the complete chain. Then check the relationship between H and J. After that, check the relationship between K and G. If the chain ensures K > G, only then 'K ≤ G' will be definitely false. Identifying the opposite symbol is important.

sections.title: Conditional Inequalities (Symbol Replacement)
sections.content: Sometimes symbols are changed. For example, @ and # are interchanged and $ is replaced with %. First perform the original decoding. Then create a new chain according to the changed symbols. Solve both situations separately. Drawing conclusions without applying the symbol change is a major mistake.

sections.title: Missing Statement Logic
sections.content: Example: M ≥ N = O ? P and the conclusion M ≥ P must be definitely true. First, M ≥ O is clear (because N = O). Now we need a relation between O and P such that M ≥ P holds in every situation. If we place O ≥ P, the chain becomes: M ≥ O ≥ P → M ≥ P is definite. Therefore, ? = ≥.

sections.title: Nested Abstract Inequalities
sections.content: Sometimes relationships are not directly between letters but between groups, such as A + B > C + D. Treat them as logical blocks. If A + B > C + D and C + D ≥ E, then A + B > E. Here, do not perform arithmetic; just understand the relational logic.

sections.title: Relationship Blockage Concept
sections.content: If opposite directions appear in the chain (for example A > B < C), then the direct relationship between A and C is blocked. In such cases, the conclusion will not be definite. Identifying blockage is very important at Level 3.

sections.title: Extreme Case Testing
sections.content: When ≥ or ≤ appears, create extreme cases. Example: X ≥ Y > Z. Consider two cases: X = Y > Z and X > Y > Z. If the conclusion is the same in both cases, only then it will be Definitely True.

sections.title: Option Elimination Strategy
sections.content: In Level 3, before finding the direct answer, eliminate wrong options. Any option that fails during decoding or creates blockage should be removed immediately. This saves time.

sections.title: 4–6 Step Evaluation Method
sections.content: Step 1: Decode the symbols. Step 2: Build the complete chain. Step 3: Identify blockage. Step 4: Check extreme cases. Step 5: Verify reverse relations. Step 6: Eliminate options and make the final decision.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Forgetting to apply symbol replacement. 2. Checking only one part in reverse conditions. 3. Treating ≥ as a single case. 4. Performing arithmetic in abstract inequalities. 5. Ignoring blockage.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: In Level 3 inequalities, decoding, reverse checking, missing link insertion, and extreme case testing are essential. Check every conclusion under multiple situations. Pay special attention to blockage and opposite directions.

tricks.title: Double Condition Check
tricks.explanation: If the question has two conditions (one true, one false), verify both separately.
tricks.example: Need H > J true and K ≤ G false → Chain must ensure K > G.

tricks.title: Symbol Swap Alert
tricks.explanation: If interchange is given, first write the symbol mapping, then solve.

tricks.title: Make the Missing Link Strong
tricks.explanation: If the conclusion must be definite, choose the missing symbol in the stronger direction.

tricks.title: Blockage Identification Trick
tricks.explanation: In A > B < C, there is no direct relationship between A and C.

tricks.title: Extreme Case Method
tricks.example: X ≥ Y > Z → In both cases X > Z

tricks.title: Think in Reverse
tricks.explanation: For a false condition, look for the opposite relation.

tricks.title: Abstract Group Handling
tricks.explanation: Treat A + B as a single block.
tricks.example: A + B > C + D and C + D > E → A + B > E

tricks.title: Eliminate Fast
tricks.explanation: Remove any option that cannot form a valid chain.
tricks.example: Reject if there is no common variable.

tricks.title: Final Line Visualization
tricks.explanation: Write the full chain in one line and compare the extremes.
